_readme: Hand-written glosses, distractors, roots and teaching notes for Esther. Generated by build-esther-glossary.mjs — edit that, not this. Entries shared with Jonah and Ruth are inherited from their glossaries at build time, so a shared word is corrected in one place. Glosses are short TEACHING meanings for a beginner reading Esther, not lexicon entries, and they flatten real semantic range. Roots are supplied only where the pairing is visible in Esther itself; Strong's derivation chains are refused. A Hebraist should read all of it.

words.notes: Turning back physically and turning from wrongdoing are the same verb — the pivot of the whole book.

words.gloss: to redeem, to act as kinsman
words.familyGloss: to redeem as next of kin

words.notes: Overlaps with יָלַךְ (H3212); the two share a paradigm between them, הָלַךְ supplying some forms and יָלַךְ others.
The name means 'pleasant'. In 1:20 she asks to be called מָרָא, 'bitter', instead.
The name is 'house of bread', and the book opens with a famine there. The pun is the narrator's, though the text never spells it out.
The divine name. Hebrew manuscripts point it with the vowels of אֲדֹנָי “Lord”, which is what is read aloud; JPS renders it “the LORD” in small capitals.
Transparently built on יָדַע 'to know' — a kinsman is one who is known — but the initial י has become ו, so no radicals are left to mark and the root is not asserted.

words.gloss: to pull out, to let fall
to be satisfied, to eat one's fill

words.notes: Distinct from חֶסֶד despite the resemblance — חסה and חסד are different roots, and only one of them means kindness.

words.gloss: to lodge, to spend the night

words.notes: Drawing off a sandal seals the transfer in 4:7, and the narrator explains the custom as already old — a note written for readers who no longer did it.

words.gloss: to draw off, to pull out

words.notes: The nearer redeemer is never named. פְּלֹנִי אַלְמֹנִי is the Hebrew for 'John Doe', and the man who refused to preserve a name does not get one.

words.familyNotes: One of the clearest root families in Hebrew: דָּבָר a word, דִּבֶּר to speak, מִדְבָּר wilderness (disputed).

words.gloss: to be stationed, to stand over
to sojourn, to live as a stranger

words.notes: Hard to translate: covenant loyalty and kindness together. Often rendered lovingkindness or steadfast love.

words.gloss: to do well, to be good
to be evil, to do harm

words.familyNotes: Not “soul” in the later philosophical sense: נֶפֶשׁ is the living, breathing self. Jonah 1:14 asks not to perish for this man's נֶפֶשׁ — his life.

words.gloss: to be determined, to strengthen oneself
to be stirred up, to be in an uproar

words.notes: The root behind אָמֵן — to be firm, to rely on.
Plural in form, singular in sense. Strong's files it under פנה “to turn”; that is an etymological guess, so no root is highlighted here.
Also means a spring of water — the same word, from the shape of the opening.
Strong's derives it from עוּר “to awake”, glossing a city as “a place guarded by waking”. That is folk etymology, so no root is marked.

words.gloss: to remain, to be left over

words.notes: Untranslatable: it marks a definite direct object rather than meaning anything itself. Strong's derives it from אוֹת “sign”, which is not correct — see the family note.
תְּמוֹל שִׁלְשׁוֹם, 'yesterday and the day before', is the idiom for 'previously'. Neither word is used alone in this sense.

words.familyNotes: The noun סַעַר and the verb סָעַר both appear in Jonah 1 — the sea storms, and there is a storm.

words.gloss: to be calm, to grow quiet

words.familyNotes: One word covers wind, breath and spirit. Jonah 1:4 has the LORD hurling a great רוּחַ onto the sea — wind, plainly, but the same word carries the other senses elsewhere.

words.notes: Related to מֶלַח “salt” — a salt-water man. Not marked as a root here, since the connection is a plausible guess rather than a paradigm.
Dual in form, like several natural pairs in Hebrew.

words.familyNotes: Verb and noun together in Jonah 1:16: וַיִּזְבְּחוּ זֶבַח — “they sacrificed a sacrifice”. Hebrew does this often, and it is not redundancy but emphasis.
The same pairing as זבח, in the same verse: וַיִּדְּרוּ נְדָרִים — “they vowed vows”.

words.notes: The realm of the dead. Not 'hell' in the later sense — Sheol is where everyone goes, without moral sorting.
In Hebrew the heart is where thinking and deciding happen, not primarily feeling.
One word for both, because a temple is a god's palace.
Dual in form, like שָׁמַיִם — Hebrew treats water as inherently plural.
The same word as in יַם־סוּף, the Sea of Reeds.
Not 'eternity' in the abstract; it means a horizon so distant it cannot be seen past.
Literally a breath or vapour. The keyword of Ecclesiastes, used here of worthless idols.
The noun behind the name Joshua, and behind Jesus.

words.familyNotes: The verb טָעַם means to taste; the noun means both a taste and a considered decision. Jonah 3:7 has the king's טַעַם — his decree — and 3:7 also forbids anyone to taste (טָעַם) anything.

words.notes: Related to אֲדָמָה, the ground — the human is the earth-creature.
Same consonants as רַע 'evil' and רֵעַ 'companion' but a different word. Unpointed Hebrew cannot tell them apart; context and vowels can.
The same word for nose and for anger — from the flaring of the nostrils. אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, 'long of nose', means slow to anger.
The plant is unidentified. Strong's guesses the castor-oil plant; the text only says it grew fast and died faster.

words.familyNotes: The same root as יַבָּשָׁה, dry land, in chapter 1 — a plant withers by the same word the sea does not cover.

words.notes: Related to אָדָם, the human — the creature made from it.

Named 58 times — more than anyone else in the book. Introduced in 2:5 with four generations of ancestry, which is how the narrator marks him as the Jew of the exile rather than a courtier who happens to be Jewish.
A Persian court name, probably from the goddess Ishtar or from Persian stara, 'star'. Her Hebrew name, given once in 2:7, is הֲדַסָּה — Hadassah, 'myrtle'.
The Hebrew spelling of Persian Khshayarsha — the king Greek writers call Xerxes. He is on stage in almost every chapter and decides almost nothing.
Haman's epithet. Agag was the Amalekite king Saul spared in 1 Samuel 15; Mordecai is a Benjamite descended from Kish, Saul's father. The two labels set an old quarrel running under the whole book.

The book's own word for its people — 58 times, more than in the whole rest of the Hebrew Bible. It names them by the province they came from, Judah, which is what an empire calls a people it has moved.
8:17 only, and the only occurrence in the Hebrew Bible: מִתְיַהֲדִים, 'were becoming Jews', after the second decree. A verb coined from the noun.
The Persian winter capital, in what is now south-western Iran. The book distinguishes שׁוּשַׁן הַבִּירָה, the fortified citadel where the court lives, from the city outside it.
The empire is measured from הֹדּוּ to כּוּשׁ — India to Cush — which is to say, from one edge of the known world to the other.
The administrative unit of the empire; the book counts 127 of them. Every decree has to be written out for each one 'in its own script and its own language'.
The commonest noun in the book by a wide margin — 196 times in 167 verses. Ahasuerus is almost never named without it.
Used both abstractly ('royal power') and attributively — כֶּתֶר מַלְכוּת 'a royal crown', בֵּית הַמַּלְכוּת 'the royal house'.
In a Persian court the word covers a class of trusted palace servants; not every סָרִיס need have been castrated, though those set over the king's women were.
A Persian loanword — the governor of a whole satrapy, above the פֶּחָה of a single district.

A Persian loanword, and the book's own term — 20 times. Note the sting in 1:19 and 8:8: a דָּת of the Medes and Persians cannot be revoked, so the second decree does not cancel the first, it only arms its victims.
9:1 turns on this verb twice in one verse: the day the enemies hoped to have power over the Jews was 'turned about' — the Jews had power over them.
The ring is the plot's hinge. The king gives it to Haman in 3:10 and to Mordecai in 8:2, and never once reads what is written with it.

words.gloss: an exact account, a full statement

words.notes: Held out to admit someone who has come uninvited (4:11, 5:2, 8:4). Touching its tip is the gesture of accepting the reprieve.
שֹׁמְרֵי הַסַּף, 'keepers of the threshold', is the title of the two doorkeepers who plot against the king in 2:21.
Literally 'a drinking'. Ten of them structure the book, from the king's 180-day feast in 1:3 to the feasting of Purim in 9:22 — and the one fast, in chapter 4, sits exactly in the middle.
1:8 only: the drinking was 'according to the law, no one compelling' — a decree that no one must be made to drink, in a book where everything else is compulsory.
February–March. The month the lot fell on, and so the month of Purim.
2:12 — each young woman's תֹּר to go in to the king, after twelve months of ointments.
2:18 only, and nowhere else in the Bible: at Esther's coronation the king grants the provinces a הֲנָחָה — a release, probably from taxes or from service.
The height of Haman's gallows — fifty cubits, some twenty-five metres. The number is meant to be absurd.

9:10, 15 and 16 each end by saying the Jews did NOT lay hands on the spoil — three times, which in Hebrew narrative means it matters. Saul's failure with Amalek in 1 Samuel 15 was exactly the opposite.
Not to be confused with בָּזָה 'to despise', which has the same three letters on the page but a different final radical.

words.gloss: to be hostile to, to oppress

words.notes: Esther uses two nearly identical nouns for the same thing in 8:6 and 9:5 — אַבְדַן and אׇבְדָן. Both mean the ruin of a people.
3:8, Haman's accusation: 'there is a certain people scattered and separated among the peoples' — the empire's own doing, described as if it were the people's fault.

words.gloss: to leave alone, to let be
words.notes: The same accusation ends 'it is not worth the king's while to tolerate them' — לְהַנִּיחָם, to leave them be.
Plain 'wood' or 'a tree'. In Esther it is always the pole Haman builds — the King James 'gallows' is an interpretation, not a translation.
A Persian loanword the narrator has to gloss for his own readers in 3:7 and 9:24: פּוּר הוּא הַגּוֹרָל, 'Pur, that is, the lot'. The feast is named after a foreign word for chance.
5:9 — Mordecai neither rose nor trembled before Haman. The refusal is physical, and it is what sets the gallows building.
3:15 puts the two side by side: the king and Haman sat down to drink, and the city of Susa was in confusion.

words.gloss: to do wrong, to go astray

words.notes: 4:3 — many lay on sackcloth and ashes; the verb is the ordinary one for spreading bedding.
8:16: 'the Jews had light and gladness and joy and honour'. Read as brightness, not literal daylight.
4:14, Mordecai's warning: relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place — the nearest the book comes to naming God.

words.gloss: to show favour, to plead for grace
to be good, to go well

words.notes: The couriers go out 'hastened and pressed' by the king's word — 3:15 and 8:14, the same phrase for both decrees.

words.gloss: a mare of the royal stud
to flee, to be driven away
words.notes: 6:1 — the king's sleep fled. Everything that follows hangs on an insomnia the narrator declines to explain.
Written exactly like שָׁנָה 'to change' and שָׁנָה 'a year'. Three unrelated words, one spelling — context is the only guide.
Only ever of the sceptre, and only in Esther — 4:11, 5:2, 8:4.

words.gloss: to receive, to take upon oneself
words.notes: 9:23 and 9:27: the Jews 'took upon themselves' the keeping of Purim. The feast is instituted by the people, not commanded from above.
3:2 — everyone in the king's gate knelt to Haman, 'but Mordecai would not kneel and would not bow'. The book never says why.
6:12 Haman goes home mourning 'with his head covered'; 7:8 the servants cover his face, which is what is done to a condemned man.
Paired with כְּתָב throughout: every decree goes out to each province 'in its own script' and to each people 'in its own tongue'.

words.gloss: to be silent, to hold one's peace
words.notes: 4:14, Mordecai to Esther: 'if you keep altogether silent at this time'. The same root elsewhere means to plough or to engrave; here it is silence.
3:8 says the Jews' laws are 'different' from every people's; 1:19 and 8:8 insist a Persian law cannot be changed. Same root, opposite directions.

words.gloss: to be worth, to be equal
words.notes: The book's accountant's verb: 3:8 'no profit to the king', 5:13 'all this is worth nothing to me', 7:4 'the adversary is not worth the king's damage'.

words.gloss: to be established, to be prepared

words.notes: Both decrees end with the same instruction — that the people be עֲתִידִים, ready, for that day. 3:14 for the killing, 8:13 for the defence.
2:1 and 7:10, both of the king's rage — the two hinges where a woman's fate is decided by a temper cooling.
2:7 — Mordecai brought up Esther, his uncle's daughter. Later Greek and Latin versions make him her cousin, which is what דֹּד־ו בַּת amounts to.
Twelve months of them before a woman goes in to the king — six with oil of myrrh, six with spices (2:12). The book states the schedule without comment.
Written מֹר. Do not confuse it with מַר 'bitter' — same two letters, different word.
2:20 — Esther kept doing as Mordecai said, as when she was under his care. The root is the one behind 'to trust' and 'amen'.
Paired with בַּקָּשָׁה every time the king asks Esther what she wants — 5:6, 5:7, 5:8, 7:2, 7:3, 9:12. She takes three chapters to answer.

3:7 casts one before Haman to fix the month, and 9:24 explains the foreign word with this native one: פּוּר הוּא הַגּוֹרָל. The feast is named after the lot, and no one in the book says who decided how it fell.

שַׁעַר הַמֶּלֶךְ, the king's gate, is where Mordecai sits in almost every chapter — the place where royal business is transacted and petitions heard, so sitting there is holding a post, not loitering.

Coarse cloth worn in mourning. Mordecai puts it on in 4:1 and walks into the city in it — and 4:2 notes that no one may enter the king's gate wearing it, which is the whole difficulty of the chapter in one clause.
In Hebrew the seat of thought and will rather than feeling. 1:10 has the king's heart 'merry with wine' and 6:6 has Haman saying in his heart — deciding, not emoting.
The book's hinge word. 9:1: on the day the enemies hoped to master the Jews, וְנַהֲפוֹךְ הוּא — 'it was overturned'. 9:22 uses it again of the month turned from sorrow to gladness.

'To find favour in the eyes of' is the ordinary idiom for being well received. Esther finds it with Hegai, with everyone who sees her, and with the king — six times, and each one decides whether she lives.
Wide: military force, wealth, or personal worth. In 1:3 it is the army of Persia and Media; in 8:11 it is the armed force of a province.
Very general: any made object. In 1:7 they are the gold drinking vessels, no two alike, at the king's feast.
2:3 — let the king appoint officers in every province. The verb covers both appointing and calling to account, which is why the same word elsewhere means to punish.
1:14 uses it of rank, not kinship: the seven princes 'near to him' are the ones who see the king's face and sit first in the kingdom.
Used with commands, where לֹא negates statements. 4:13, Mordecai to Esther: אַל־תְּדַמִּי — 'do not imagine you will escape in the king's house'.
